transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Alex Park (CTO, Streamline), Samira Khan (ML Eng), Jordan Lee (SRE), Priya Patel (Security)

Auto-summary: SE-led walkthrough of throughput tuning knobs for real-time inference. Talk covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler settings, max_num_seqs, token limits and KV cache interactions. Action items captured at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you making time. Quick intros?
[00:08] Alex Park: Alex here, CTO at Streamline Health, we run patient-facing summarization and routing pipelines, lots of variable length requests.
[00:15] Samira Khan: Hi I'm Samira, ML eng, I own model infra and perf.
[00:20] Jordan Lee: Jordan, SRE, I'll handle cluster/network stuff.
[00:25] Priya Patel: Priya, security — quick on compliance questions.
[00:30] Diego Ramos: Diego from Redwood, SE on the runtime team, I did the tuning work we will go over today.

[00:45] Maya Chen: Goal for today is to go deeper into throughput knobs — continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, and how KV cache and quantization affect latency and cost. We'll leave time for Q&A.

[01:12] Diego Ramos: Cool, jumping in. Quick recap: continuous batching is our default scheduler mode for low-latency, high-throughput workloads. It accumulates in-flight sequences and dispatches micro-batches to the GPU based on latency budget and max_num_seqs. Key knobs: max_num_seqs, batch_timeout_ms, and max_total_tokens_per_batch.
[01:40] Diego Ramos: For Streamline's traffic where median seq len is ~60 tokens but 95th is ~400, you want to bias toward a lower max_num_seqs to avoid token blowup on long requests.
[02:05] Samira Khan: Can you clarify token blowup? We saw throughput drop in our test when a single long request hit.
[02:12] Diego Ramos: Yeah, when a long seq enters it holds the KV cache for that beam and increases the total token count in the batch — if max_num_seqs is high, you accumulate many seqs, but total tokens explode and triggers out of memory or huge per-batch latency.
[02:35] Alex Park: So what's the rough heuristic? Lower seqs or caps?
[02:40] Diego Ramos: Heuristics we use: set max_num_seqs to 4-8 for mixed short/long workloads on A100/H100 families, and enforce a max_total_tokens_per_batch of ~4096-8192 depending on memory headroom. Also set batch_timeout_ms low (10-30ms) for interactive workloads so we don't wait too long to fill large token-heavy batches.
[03:08] Jordan Lee: On our side, we have strict tail-latency SLOs — if you lower max_num_seqs that reduces throughput, right? We're trying to balance cost too.
[03:18] Diego Ramos: Exactly, it's a tradeoff. Lower max_num_seqs increases GPU utilization inefficiency but reduces tail latency and OOM risk. Continuous batching combined with adaptive token caps helps — the scheduler can prefer packing by token count rather than sequence count.
[03:45] Samira Khan: Is that an exposed switch? Adaptive by token count?
[03:48] Diego Ramos: Yes, we have scheduler_mode: sequence_count | token_count | hybrid. Hybrid will try to keep sequences small but cap by tokens. For streaming/real-time we recommend hybrid.
[04:05] Priya Patel: Quick sec on security, if we change scheduler behavior does that impact data residency, logs, or KV cache persistence?
[04:14] Diego Ramos: Good Q. No change to residency — request metadata and KV cache stay ephemeral per-request; the scheduler only packs requests on the compute nodes. Audit logs and request traces are unaffected; KMS keys and HSM workflow remain the same for private deployments. We'll send the security doc with those details.
[04:38] Maya Chen: Diego, can you show the config example and the numbers you used in the benchmark?
[04:44] Diego Ramos: Sure, pulling up the slide. Example: scheduler_mode=hybrid, max_num_seqs=6, max_total_tokens_per_batch=8192, batch_timeout_ms=25, prefix_cache_enabled=true, kv_ttl_ms=60000. Quantization profile: 4-bit LLMQ for embeddings, 8-bit for generation in sensitive pipelines. We saw 18-22% cost drop with negligible latency change in gen-optimized models.
[05:20] Samira Khan: For quantization you said 4-bit for embeddings — we're concerned about quality regression on summarization. Any eval guidance?
[05:28] Diego Ramos: Test with your prompt sets — quantization has different impact by architecture. Our recommendation: run shadow eval (embedding space drift + downstream summarization eval) with a 1% sample, and flag any >2% drop in ROUGE/BERTScore. We can help run that.
[05:55] Alex Park: On the KV cache — are prefix caches shared across requests or per-customer? We have PHI concerns.
[06:02] Diego Ramos: Per-customer, per-instance ephemeral caches. For private deployments in your VPC the data never leaves your network; logs can be configured to scrub, and we support zero-logging mode for highly regulated flows.
[06:20] Jordan Lee: About the benchmarks you ran, what hardware and concurrency? We need comparable numbers to our on-prem H100 racks.
[06:28] Diego Ramos: We ran on 4xH100 (80GB) and 8xA100 (80GB) testbeds. Load generator replayed your production token distribution (thanks for sample). For the H100 with scheduler_mode=hybrid and max_num_seqs=6 we got steady-state throughput of ~1.4M tokens/min across the pool and median per-request latency 120-160ms for short requests. For A100 pool it was ~900k tokens/min with slightly higher tail.
[06:58] Samira Khan: Those numbers look good. If we drop max_num_seqs to 3 what happens?
[07:04] Diego Ramos: Throughput drops ~10-18% but p99 latency improves by 30-40% for mixed workloads. That's why hybrid + token caps is useful — you avoid big long-request spikes.
[07:20] Maya Chen: There's also the batch_timeout_ms setting — is that applied per-queue? Can we have different latency tiers?
[07:26] Diego Ramos: Yes per-route configs. You can map latency-sensitive routes to lower batch_timeout_ms and lower max_num_seqs, and background jobs to higher allowances with larger batching.
[07:40] Alex Park: For our multi-tenant internal app we want isolation — is dedicated capacity better than hosted? We like Redwood's dedicated offering but want to confirm implications for tuning.
[07:51] Diego Ramos: With dedicated you get predictable throughput and you can tune at the node level. Some knobs (like KV cache TTL) are available both hosted and dedicated, but dedicated gives you control over pool size and node types; that matters for max_num_seqs choices because memory headroom differs.
[08:10] Jordan Lee: On VPC/on-prem, you'll need access to our staging cluster — what's the integration path?
[08:16] Maya Chen: We'll do an on-prem pilot: Redwood provides a private control plane and an agent for the inference nodes; Jordan will share temporary VPC access and we can run the benchmark in your staging.
[08:30] Priya Patel: We'll need SOC2 artifact review and encryption details before we grant broad access.
[08:36] Maya Chen: Absolutely, we'll attach the security pack.
[08:40] Diego Ramos: Back to tuning — we also recommended token limit per-request (max_request_tokens). For Streamline's use case we suggested setting max_request_tokens to 1024 for interactive summarization; that prevents runaway generations and caps KV size.
[09:00] Samira Khan: For long form summarization sometimes you need >1024, how to handle?
[09:06] Diego Ramos: Either route those to an offline batch pipeline with higher batch caps, or use chunked generation with prefix caching so each chunk benefits from KV reuse without blowing memory.
[09:20] Alex Park: Any gotchas with prefix_cache_enabled=true? We saw cache hits sometimes not improving throughput.
[09:27] Diego Ramos: Cache hit rate depends on prefix similarity and request alignment. If your requests have heavy personalization, cache may not help. Also cache eviction and TTL settings matter; if TTL too low you get churn. We saw best results with kv_ttl_ms around 30-120s for interactive apps.
[09:50] Jordan Lee: Can we measure KV cache hit rate per-route?
[09:54] Diego Ramos: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route cache hit metrics, plus token-level cost breakdown. We'll share dashboard links in the follow-up.
[10:05] Samira Khan: What about scheduler preemption or fairness between customers on shared pools?
[10:10] Diego Ramos: Scheduler supports priority classes and weights; highest priority routes preempt lower ones within configured budgets. For multi-tenant hosted pools we use weight-based scheduling; for Dedicated you can reserve capacity.
[10:25] Alex Park: We also want to test quantized models — what's the impact on latency?
[10:30] Diego Ramos: 4-bit quantization reduces memory and can increase throughput because you fit larger batches, but per-token execution might slightly increase due to dequant/quant ops. Net effect in our tests was 10-25% cost reduction with 5-12% median latency change depending on model. Always validate quality.
[10:54] Samira Khan: On realism of tests — we need the benchmark harness you used.
[10:58] Diego Ramos: We'll provide the harness (open-source) plus a config file that maps to your traces. It replays arrival times and token lengths, including jitter. The commands are in the spreadsheet we'll send.
[11:15] Jordan Lee: For the VPC agent, are there firewall rules or ports we need to open?
[11:21] Diego Ramos: Minimal: outbound TLS to the control plane on 443 and internal cluster ports for gRPC. We'll provide an ACL doc.
[11:33] Priya Patel: Curious on audit logs retention — can we set shorter retention?
[11:37] Maya Chen: Yes per-account retention policies available for Private deployments; hosted has tiers and we can discuss enterprise options.
[11:48] Alex Park: Any other scheduler knobs beyond the ones you mentioned?
[11:51] Diego Ramos: There's also max_concurrent_sequences_per_gpu, per-node token_budget, dynamic_batch_shrink (which reduces batch size when tokens spike), and prefetch_kv which preloads frequently used prefixes on warm nodes. We'll annotate these in the config doc.
[12:10] Samira Khan: Dynamic_batch_shrink sounds useful. How is the threshold set?
[12:14] Diego Ramos: It's based on observed token rate — by default it triggers when total_tokens_in_batch > 0.8 * token_budget. Threshold is configurable.
[12:25] Jordan Lee: For our on-prem H100s, any recommended defaults?
[12:29] Diego Ramos: For 4xH100 we recommended: max_num_seqs=6, token_budget=8192, batch_timeout_ms=20, scheduler_mode=hybrid, dynamic_batch_shrink=true. For 8xA100: max_num_seqs=4, token_budget=6144. Those are starting points; we'll tune after replay.
[12:55] Samira Khan: Ok, can we talk about p99 latencies? We need to hit <500ms p99 for interactive.
[13:02] Diego Ramos: With the above settings and hybrid mode we saw p99 ~320-420ms on H100 for your traces; with lower max_num_seqs you can get p99 <300ms at cost of throughput.
[13:20] Alex Park: Good. Any failure modes we should watch when rolling out?
[13:24] Diego Ramos: OOMs during spikes, and sudden throughput drops if a long-running request saturates the KV cache. We recommend circuit-breaker rules: max_request_tokens, route timeouts, and auto-fallback to a smaller model variant on overload.
[13:44] Maya Chen: Let's capture the rollout plan: run benchmark, tune config, then canary for 6 hours, monitor p90/p99 and cache hit rate, then ramp to full.
[13:55] Alex Park: Sounds good.
[14:00] Diego Ramos: Any last questions?
[14:03] Priya Patel: Security doc timeline?
[14:05] Maya Chen: We'll send the SOC2 + KMS/HSM details in the next email, targeted EOD tomorrow.
[14:12] Samira Khan: One more: how do we handle very bursty periods — like 5x baseline traffic for 10 minutes?
[14:20] Diego Ramos: Autoscaling and burst capacity policies are key — for dedicated we recommend reserve burst nodes and a pre-warmed pool; for hosted we have cross-region failover and lower-cost spillover models to handle brief bursts. Also ensure queue depth limits and request throttles on client side.
[14:45] Jordan Lee: We'll provide production traces and open the staging VPC as requested.
[14:50] Maya Chen: Great — I'll follow up with the spreadsheet, scheduler examples, and a proposed benchmark window.
[14:57] Diego Ramos: Thanks everyone, we'll start the benchmark once we have traces.
[15:00] Alex Park: Thanks team, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
